title: AI Calculators and Interactive Decision Tools
answer: Six interactive estimators for the questions that decide whether an AI project is viable: token cost, GPU memory, context window fit, training cost, energy and carbon, and return on investment. Each shows its own arithmetic and states what it excludes.

reading.body:
Six interactive estimators cover the questions that decide whether an AI project is viable: token cost, GPU memory, context window fit, training cost, energy and carbon, and return on investment.

The set is a decision layer rather than a measurement layer. Each tool shows its own arithmetic and states what it excludes, which means the output is a range a reader can inspect, not a benchmark result. The six questions map onto the cost stack in order: what inference costs per token, whether the model fits in the memory you can buy, whether the input fits in the context window, what training costs, what the energy and carbon come to, and whether any of it returns more than it spends.

For AI specifically, the interesting grouping is that memory, context, and energy sit alongside cost and return. Those three are physical constraints, not financial ones. A project can clear its budget and still fail because the weights do not fit on the available GPUs or the power draw is not there. Putting them in the same set of estimators treats the physical limits as first-class inputs to the viability question.

What the data does not cover is any result. There are no computed values here, no worked examples, and no indication of what inputs the estimators accept or how current their assumptions are. The tools are dated 2026-10-09 and scheduled to refresh every seven days, so the arithmetic is meant to track changing prices and hardware. Nothing in the data says how accurate any estimator is against a real bill.
